description: MATLAB's tabular data containers: tables for heterogeneous column-oriented data, timetables for time-stamped rows, and categorical arrays for labelled discrete values. Covers construction and conversion, variable management, grouped computation, reshaping, joining, time alignment and resampling.

tools.name: table
tools.description: Creates a table, a container whose columns (variables) can each have a different data type but must share the same number of rows. Variables are accessed by name with dot notation, and rows can carry names or, in a timetable, times. Use tables for mixed-type data sets such as measurements with labels, units and timestamps.
tools.usage:
T = table(var1, ..., varN)
T = table(___, 'VariableNames', names)
T = table(___, 'RowNames', rowNames)
T = table('Size', sz, 'VariableTypes', types)

parameters.name: var1,...,varN
parameters.description: Column variables, all with the same number of rows.

parameters.name: 'VariableNames'
parameters.description: Cell array or string array of variable names.

parameters.name: 'RowNames'
parameters.description: Names identifying each row.

parameters.name: 'Size'/'VariableTypes'
parameters.description: Preallocate an empty table of a given size and types.

tools.notes: T(1,:) returns a table while T{1,2} returns the raw value and T.age returns the whole column; keeping these three indexing forms straight is the main learning curve. Table variables can themselves be matrices, so one variable may span several columns.

tools.name: array2table
tools.description: Converts a numeric or logical matrix to a table, creating one variable per column with automatic or supplied names. Use it after a numeric computation when you want named columns for display, export or joining. All the resulting variables share the class of the input matrix.
tools.usage:
T = array2table(A)
T = array2table(A, 'VariableNames', names)
T = array2table(A, 'RowNames', rowNames)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Matrix to convert.

parameters.name: 'VariableNames'
parameters.description: Names for the resulting variables.

parameters.name: 'RowNames'
parameters.description: Row identifiers.

tools.notes: Default names are Var1, Var2 and so on. Names that are not valid MATLAB identifiers are allowed but must be accessed with the T.('name with space') syntax.

tools.name: cell2table
tools.description: Converts a cell array to a table, with each column becoming one variable and homogeneous columns automatically concatenated into arrays. Use it after reading heterogeneous data with `textscan` or building results in a cell array. Columns whose contents cannot be concatenated remain cell variables.
tools.usage:
T = cell2table(C)
T = cell2table(C, 'VariableNames', names)
T = cell2table(C, 'RowNames', rowNames)

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Cell array; each column becomes a table variable.

parameters.name: 'VariableNames'
parameters.description: Names for the variables.

tools.notes: Character vectors become a cell variable rather than a string array; convert afterwards with `convertvars(T, 'name', 'string')`. Mixed-type columns stay as cells.

tools.name: struct2table
tools.description: Converts a structure array to a table, mapping each field to a table variable and each struct element to a row. Use it to tabulate the output of functions that return struct arrays, such as `dir`, and to make struct data easier to filter and display. The reverse conversion is `table2struct`.
tools.usage:
T = struct2table(S)
T = struct2table(S, 'AsArray', tf)
T = struct2table(S, 'RowNames', rowNames)

parameters.name: S
parameters.description: Structure array.

parameters.name: 'AsArray'
parameters.description: true to treat a scalar struct as a single row rather than expanding its fields.

tools.notes: A scalar struct whose fields hold column vectors is expanded into multiple rows unless you pass 'AsArray', true, which is a frequent surprise.

tools.name: table2array
tools.description: Converts a table to a homogeneous array by horizontally concatenating all its variables. Use it to hand tabular data to numeric functions that do not accept tables. All variables must be concatenation-compatible, so mixed numeric and text tables fail.
tools.usage: A = table2array(T)

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: Table whose variables can be concatenated.

tools.notes: Concatenating numeric with string variables yields a string array rather than an error, which silently changes the type. `T{:,:}` is the shorter equivalent, and `T{:, vars}` selects a subset.

tools.name: table2struct
tools.description: Converts a table to a structure array, one element per row with one field per variable, or to a scalar struct of columns when 'ToScalar' is true. Use it when passing tabular data to code that expects structs, or to build JSON-friendly records for `jsonencode`. Row names can be carried into a field.
tools.usage:
S = table2struct(T)
S = table2struct(T, 'ToScalar', tf)

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: Table to convert.

parameters.name: 'ToScalar'
parameters.description: true to produce one struct whose fields are whole columns.

tools.notes: The row-per-element form is the right shape for JSON arrays of objects; the scalar form suits column-oriented consumers.

tools.name: readtable
tools.description: Reads tabular data from delimited text, spreadsheet, XML, HTML, Parquet or fixed-width files into a table, detecting delimiters, headers and variable types automatically. Import options objects give precise control over which rows and variables to read and how to treat missing and error values. It is the standard entry point for loading data files into MATLAB.
tools.usage:
T = readtable(filename)
T = readtable(filename, Name, Value)
T = readtable(filename, opts)
opts = detectImportOptions(filename)

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Path to a .csv, .txt, .xlsx, .xml, .html, .parquet or similar file.

parameters.name: 'Sheet', 'Range'
parameters.description: Spreadsheet sheet name or number and cell range.

parameters.name: 'Delimiter'
parameters.description: Field delimiter for text files.

parameters.name: 'ReadVariableNames'
parameters.description: Whether the first row holds variable names.

parameters.name: 'VariableNamingRule'
parameters.description: 'modify' or 'preserve' to keep original column headings.

parameters.name: 'TextType'
parameters.description: 'char' (default in older releases) or 'string'.

tools.notes: Always inspect `detectImportOptions` output on unfamiliar files; automatic type detection samples only part of the file and can guess wrong. Use 'VariableNamingRule','preserve' to keep column headings that are not valid identifiers.

tools.name: writetable
tools.description: Writes a table or timetable to a delimited text file, spreadsheet, XML or Parquet file, inferring the format from the extension. Options control the delimiter, whether variable names and row names are written, and which sheet and range to use. Use it to export results for other tools or for archiving.
tools.usage:
writetable(T)
writetable(T, filename)
writetable(T, filename, Name, Value)

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Output file; the extension selects the format.

parameters.name: 'Delimiter'
parameters.description: Field separator for text output.

parameters.name: 'WriteVariableNames'
parameters.description: Whether to write a header row; default true.

parameters.name: 'WriteRowNames'
parameters.description: Whether to write row names as the first column.

parameters.name: 'Sheet', 'Range'
parameters.description: Spreadsheet destination.

parameters.name: 'WriteMode'
parameters.description: 'overwrite' (default), 'append', 'overwritesheet' or 'inplace'.

tools.notes: Appending to a CSV writes the header again unless you set 'WriteVariableNames' to false. Writing spreadsheets on a machine without Excel uses a built-in writer that supports a subset of formatting.

tools.name: summary
tools.description: Prints or returns a per-variable summary of a table or timetable: class, minimum, median and maximum for numeric data, category counts for categorical data, and the number of missing values. Use it as the first step when exploring an unfamiliar data set. Requesting an output gives a struct you can inspect programmatically.
tools.usage:
summary(T)
s = summary(T)
summary(T, dim)

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: Table, timetable or categorical array.

tools.notes: The printed form is for human reading; the struct form is what you script against. For quick shape information use `height`, `width` and `size` instead.

tools.name: head
tools.description: Returns the first rows of a table, timetable or array, eight by default. Use it to inspect large data sets without printing everything, and to check that an import produced what you expected. `tail` returns the last rows with the same syntax.
tools.usage:
B = head(A)
B = head(A, k)
B = tail(A, k)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Table, timetable or array.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Number of rows; defaults to 8.

tools.example:
T = array2table(rand(100, 3));
head(T)
head(T, 3)
tail(T, 2)
height(T)
tools.notes: For tall arrays and datastores, head is the cheap way to preview data without triggering a full pass. Requesting more rows than exist simply returns everything.

tools.name: height
tools.description: Returns the number of rows in a table, timetable or array, which is size(A,1). Use it in loops and validation instead of size, because it reads more clearly for tabular data. `width` returns the number of variables.
tools.usage:
H = height(T)
W = width(T)

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: Table, timetable or array.

tools.example:
T = table((1:5)', rand(5,1));
height(T)
width(T)
size(T)
for k = 1:height(T), disp(T.Var1(k)); end
tools.notes: For a table, `width` counts variables, not columns, so a variable that is itself an n-column matrix still counts as one. `size(T,2)` agrees with width.

tools.name: addvars
tools.description: Adds one or more variables to a table or timetable at a chosen position, either before or after a named variable. Use it to build up tables in a readable pipeline instead of assigning into dot-named fields and then reordering. Names for the new variables can be supplied in the call.
tools.usage:
T2 = addvars(T1, var1, ..., varN)
T2 = addvars(___, 'Before', location)
T2 = addvars(___, 'After', location)
T2 = addvars(___, 'NewVariableNames', names)

parameters.name: var1,...,varN
parameters.description: Variables to add; each must have height(T1) rows.

parameters.name: 'Before'/'After'
parameters.description: Variable name or index defining the insertion point.

parameters.name: 'NewVariableNames'
parameters.description: Names for the added variables.

tools.example:
T = table([1;2;3], [4;5;6], 'VariableNames', {'a','b'});
T = addvars(T, T.a + T.b, 'NewVariableNames', 'total')
T = addvars(T, [10;20;30], 'Before', 'a', 'NewVariableNames', 'id')
T.Properties.VariableNames
tools.notes: Without 'NewVariableNames' the added variables get default names like Var3. `removevars`, `movevars`, `renamevars` and `convertvars` complete the variable-management family.

tools.name: removevars
tools.description: Deletes one or more variables from a table or timetable by name, index or logical mask. Use it to drop columns you no longer need before exporting or joining. It is clearer and safer than assigning [] into a variable.
tools.usage: T2 = removevars(T1, vars)

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variable names, indices, or a logical vector selecting variables to remove.

tools.notes: The alternative `T.Var2 = []` works but reads poorly and cannot remove several variables at once. Removing a variable that does not exist raises an error.

tools.name: movevars
tools.description: Moves table variables to a new position, before or after another variable. Use it to arrange columns for display and export without rebuilding the table. The data is untouched; only the variable order changes.
tools.usage:
T2 = movevars(T1, vars, 'Before', location)
T2 = movevars(T1, vars, 'After', location)

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variables to move, by name or index.

parameters.name: 'Before'/'After'
parameters.description: Target location variable.

tools.notes: You can also reorder with subscripting, `T = T(:, {'c','a','b'})`, which is equivalent but requires listing every variable.

tools.name: renamevars
tools.description: Renames table or timetable variables, taking lists of old and new names. Use it to normalize column names after import, for example converting spreadsheet headings into valid identifiers. It is clearer than assigning into the VariableNames property when only a few names change.
tools.usage: T2 = renamevars(T1, vars, newNames)

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Existing variable names or indices.

parameters.name: newNames
parameters.description: New names, one per entry in vars.

tools.notes: Available since R2020a. Names must be unique within the table; duplicates raise an error.

tools.name: convertvars
tools.description: Converts selected table variables to a specified data type in one call, accepting a type name or a conversion function handle. Use it to turn imported text columns into categorical, string or datetime after reading a file. Variable selection can use names, indices, a logical mask or a type-testing function.
tools.usage: T2 = convertvars(T1, vars, dataType)

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variables to convert: names, indices, a logical mask, or a function handle such as @isnumeric.

parameters.name: dataType
parameters.description: Target class name or a conversion function handle.

tools.notes: Passing @iscellstr or @isnumeric as the vars selector converts every variable of that kind, which is handy right after import. Conversions that fail raise an error rather than producing missing values.

tools.name: varfun
tools.description: Applies a function to each variable of a table separately, optionally within groups, returning a table or an array. Use it to compute per-column statistics, to inspect variable classes, and to transform every numeric column at once. The GroupingVariables option turns it into a grouped aggregation.
tools.usage:
B = varfun(func, A)
B = varfun(func, A, Name, Value)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function handle applied to each variable.

parameters.name: 'InputVariables'
parameters.description: Which variables to process.

parameters.name: 'GroupingVariables'
parameters.description: Variables that define groups.

parameters.name: 'OutputFormat'
parameters.description: 'table' (default), 'uniform' or 'cell'.

tools.example:
T = table([1;2;3;4], [10;20;30;40], categorical(["a";"a";"b";"b"]), 'VariableNames', {'x','y','g'});
varfun(@mean, T, 'InputVariables', {'x','y'})
varfun(@mean, T, 'GroupingVariables', 'g', 'InputVariables', {'x','y'})
varfun(@class, T, 'OutputFormat', 'cell')
tools.notes: Output variable names get a prefix such as mean_x. `rowfun` applies a function across variables within each row instead, and `groupsummary` is usually more convenient for grouped statistics.

tools.name: rowfun
tools.description: Applies a function to each row of a table, or to each group of rows, passing the selected variables as separate input arguments. Use it when a computation combines several columns, such as computing a derived quantity per observation. Output variable names and formats are configurable.
tools.usage:
B = rowfun(func, A)
B = rowfun(func, A, Name, Value)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function handle taking one argument per input variable.

parameters.name: 'InputVariables'
parameters.description: Variables passed to func.

parameters.name: 'GroupingVariables'
parameters.description: Variables defining groups; func then receives whole columns.

parameters.name: 'OutputVariableNames'
parameters.description: Names for the results.

parameters.name: 'NumOutputs'
parameters.description: How many outputs func returns.

parameters.name: 'SeparateInputs'
parameters.description: false to pass all inputs as one row vector.

tools.notes: rowfun calls the function once per row, so it is much slower than vectorized column arithmetic; prefer `T.r = hypot(T.a, T.b)` when the operation vectorizes.

tools.name: findgroups
tools.description: Assigns a consecutive integer group number to each row based on one or more grouping variables, and returns the unique group identifiers as a second output. It is the companion of `splitapply` for split-apply-combine workflows. Use it when you want explicit control over the grouping before aggregating.
tools.usage:
G = findgroups(A)
[G, ID] = findgroups(A)
[G, ID1, ID2] = findgroups(A1, A2)
[G, TID] = findgroups(T)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Grouping variable: numeric, categorical, string, datetime or a table of such variables.

tools.notes: Rows with missing grouping values get group number NaN and are excluded by `splitapply`. Group numbering follows the sorted order of the unique group values.

tools.name: splitapply
tools.description: Splits data into groups defined by group numbers from `findgroups`, applies a function to each group, and concatenates the results. Use it for custom aggregations that `groupsummary` does not provide, such as fitting a model per group or returning several values per group. The function receives each group's data as one column vector per input.
tools.usage:
Y = splitapply(func, X, G)
Y = splitapply(func, X1, ..., XN, G)
[Y1, ..., YM] = splitapply(___)
Y = splitapply(func, T, G)

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Function applied to each group's data.

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Data to split; a table or one or more arrays.

parameters.name: G
parameters.description: Group numbers from `findgroups`.

tools.notes: If the function returns a non-scalar, wrap it in a cell with `@(x) {f(x)}` so the results can be concatenated. Group order follows the numbering from findgroups.

tools.name: groupsummary
tools.description: Computes grouped summary statistics on a table, timetable or array in one call, supporting built-in methods such as mean, median, sum and nnz as well as custom function handles. It can also bin a continuous grouping variable automatically, including by time units for datetimes. Use it as the default tool for aggregation, falling back to findgroups and splitapply for unusual cases.
tools.usage:
G = groupsummary(T, groupvars)
G = groupsummary(T, groupvars, method)
G = groupsummary(T, groupvars, method, datavars)
G = groupsummary(T, groupvars, groupbins, method, datavars)

parameters.name: groupvars
parameters.description: Variables that define the groups.

parameters.name: groupbins
parameters.description: Bin edges, a bin count, or a time unit such as 'month' for a datetime grouping variable.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: 'sum', 'mean', 'median', 'max', 'min', 'range', 'std', 'nnz', 'numunique', 'none', or a function handle.

parameters.name: datavars
parameters.description: Which variables to summarize.

parameters.name: 'IncludeEmptyGroups'
parameters.description: Include groups with no members.

tools.notes: A GroupCount variable is always added so you can see how many rows contributed. Binning a datetime by 'month' or 'week' is much simpler than constructing the bins by hand.

tools.name: sortrows
tools.description: Sorts the rows of a matrix, table or timetable by one or more columns or variables, keeping each row intact. Direction can be set per key, and ties are broken by later keys. Use it for ranking, for preparing data for grouped operations, and before writing ordered output.
tools.usage:
B = sortrows(A)
B = sortrows(A, column)
B = sortrows(T, vars)
B = sortrows(___, direction)
[B, index] = sortrows(___)

parameters.name: column
parameters.description: Column numbers for a matrix; negative values sort descending.

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variable names or indices for a table.

parameters.name: direction
parameters.description: 'ascend' or 'descend', scalar or one per key.

parameters.name: 'MissingPlacement'
parameters.description: 'auto', 'first' or 'last'.

tools.notes: Sorting a timetable by row times uses `sortrows(TT)` with no key. The second output gives the permutation, which you can apply to other arrays to keep them aligned.

tools.name: stack
tools.description: Reshapes a table from wide to tall format, combining several variables into one data variable plus an indicator variable naming the source. Use it to convert one-column-per-condition layouts into the long format that grouped analysis and many plotting functions expect. `unstack` performs the inverse transformation.
tools.usage:
S = stack(T, vars)
S = stack(T, vars, Name, Value)
[S, iu] = stack(___)

parameters.name: vars
parameters.description: Variables to combine into one.

parameters.name: 'NewDataVariableName'
parameters.description: Name for the stacked data variable.

parameters.name: 'IndexVariableName'
parameters.description: Name for the indicator variable.

parameters.name: 'ConstantVariables'
parameters.description: Variables to repeat for every stacked row.

tools.notes: The indicator variable is categorical, which makes it immediately usable as a grouping variable. Stacking variables of different types is not allowed.

tools.name: unstack
tools.description: Reshapes a table from tall to wide format, spreading the values of one data variable into several new variables named by the levels of an indicator variable. Use it to build cross-tabulations and pivot-table style summaries. An aggregation function handles cases where several rows map to the same output cell.
tools.usage:
U = unstack(S, dataVar, indVar)
U = unstack(S, dataVar, indVar, Name, Value)

parameters.name: dataVar
parameters.description: Variable holding the values to spread.

parameters.name: indVar
parameters.description: Variable whose levels become new variable names.

parameters.name: 'AggregationFunction'
parameters.description: Function applied when several rows share a cell.

parameters.name: 'GroupingVariables'
parameters.description: Variables identifying the output rows.

tools.notes: Cells with no corresponding row become missing values. Indicator levels that are not valid identifiers are modified to form variable names.

tools.name: rows2vars
tools.description: Transposes a table so that its rows become variables and its variables become rows, carrying the old variable names into a new column. Use it to reorient summary tables for display, and to turn a table of parameters into one row per case. Variables must be compatible for concatenation after transposition.
tools.usage:
T2 = rows2vars(T1)
T2 = rows2vars(T1, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'VariableNamingRow'
parameters.description: Row whose values become the new variable names.

parameters.name: 'VariableNamesSource'
parameters.description: Variable whose values become the new variable names.

parameters.name: 'DataVariables'
parameters.description: Which variables to transpose.

tools.notes: Mixed-type tables become cell or string variables after transposition, since a single column must hold one type. The original variable names land in a variable called OriginalVariableNames by default.

tools.name: innerjoin
tools.description: Combines two tables by matching values in one or more key variables, keeping only rows that have a match in both. It is the SQL inner join for MATLAB tables. Use it to attach lookup information to a data table when unmatched rows should be dropped.
tools.usage:
T = innerjoin(Tleft, Tright)
T = innerjoin(Tleft, Tright, Name, Value)
[T, ileft, iright] = innerjoin(___)

parameters.name: 'Keys'
parameters.description: Variables to match on; common variable names are used by default.

parameters.name: 'LeftKeys', 'RightKeys'
parameters.description: Key variables when their names differ.

parameters.name: 'LeftVariables', 'RightVariables'
parameters.description: Which variables to carry into the result.

tools.notes: Rows can be duplicated when keys are not unique, producing a result larger than either input. `join` requires unique keys in the second table and preserves the row order of the first.

tools.name: outerjoin
tools.description: Combines two tables by matching key variables, keeping unmatched rows from one or both sides and filling the missing variables with missing values. Set the Type option to 'left', 'right' or 'full' to choose which unmatched rows survive. Use it when you must not lose records that lack a counterpart.
tools.usage:
T = outerjoin(Tleft, Tright)
T = outerjoin(Tleft, Tright, Name, Value)
[T, ileft, iright] = outerjoin(___)

parameters.name: 'Keys'
parameters.description: Key variables to match on.

parameters.name: 'Type'
parameters.description: 'full' (default), 'left' or 'right'.

parameters.name: 'MergeKeys'
parameters.description: true to merge the left and right key variables into one.

parameters.name: 'LeftVariables', 'RightVariables'
parameters.description: Variables to include in the output.

tools.notes: Without 'MergeKeys' you get both id_left and id_right variables, one of which is missing for unmatched rows. Check for missing values afterwards with `ismissing`.

tools.name: timetable
tools.description: Creates a timetable, a table whose rows are indexed by a datetime or duration row-time vector. Row times enable time-based subscripting, resampling, synchronization and time-aware smoothing. Use it for any time series with one or more variables measured at the same instants.
tools.usage:
TT = timetable(rowTimes, var1, ..., varN)
TT = timetable(var1, ..., varN, 'RowTimes', rowTimes)
TT = timetable(var1, ..., varN, 'SampleRate', fs)
TT = timetable(var1, ..., varN, 'TimeStep', dt)

parameters.name: rowTimes
parameters.description: Datetime or duration vector of row times.

parameters.name: 'SampleRate'
parameters.description: Regular sampling rate in Hz.

parameters.name: 'TimeStep'
parameters.description: Regular time step as a duration or calendarDuration.

parameters.name: 'StartTime'
parameters.description: Time of the first row for regular timetables.

tools.notes: Row times must be unique for most operations but do not have to be sorted; use `sortrows` and `unique` first if they are not. `isregular` reports whether the spacing is uniform, which `retime` and `synchronize` care about.

tools.name: table2timetable
tools.description: Converts a table to a timetable by designating one variable as the row times, or by supplying a separate time vector. Use it after reading a data file whose timestamps arrived as an ordinary variable. `timetable2table` converts back, optionally keeping the row times as a variable.
tools.usage:
TT = table2timetable(T)
TT = table2timetable(T, 'RowTimes', timeVar)
T = timetable2table(TT)
T = timetable2table(TT, 'ConvertRowTimes', tf)

parameters.name: T
parameters.description: Table to convert.

parameters.name: 'RowTimes'
parameters.description: Name, index or vector giving the row times.

parameters.name: 'ConvertRowTimes'
parameters.description: For the reverse conversion, whether to keep row times as a variable.

tools.notes: If the table already has exactly one datetime or duration variable, table2timetable uses it automatically. The row-time variable is removed from the variable list and becomes the time dimension.

tools.name: retime
tools.description: Resamples or aggregates a timetable onto a new set of row times, using interpolation, fill rules or aggregation methods such as mean and sum. Use it to convert irregular measurements to a regular grid, to downsample to hourly or daily statistics, and to fill gaps. New times can be given explicitly or as a time step or unit name.
tools.usage:
TT2 = retime(TT1, newTimes)
TT2 = retime(TT1, newTimeStep)
TT2 = retime(TT1, method)
TT2 = retime(TT1, newTimes, method)

parameters.name: newTimes
parameters.description: Explicit datetime or duration vector for the output rows.

parameters.name: newTimeStep
parameters.description: 'hourly', 'daily', 'monthly', 'regular' and similar unit names.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: 'fillwithmissing', 'previous', 'next', 'nearest', 'linear', 'spline', 'pchip', 'makima', or an aggregation such as 'mean', 'sum', 'max', 'min', 'count'.

parameters.name: 'TimeStep'
parameters.description: Explicit duration step for a regular output grid.

tools.notes: Interpolation methods produce a value at every new time, while aggregation methods summarize the values falling in each new interval. Check for NaN in the result when the new grid extends beyond the data.

tools.name: synchronize
tools.description: Combines two or more timetables onto a common time vector, resampling or aggregating each as needed. Use it to align sensors that sample at different rates or offsets before joint analysis. The time vector can be the union, intersection, first, last, or a regular grid of your choosing.
tools.usage:
TT = synchronize(TT1, TT2)
TT = synchronize(TT1, TT2, newTimeBasis)
TT = synchronize(TT1, TT2, newTimeBasis, method)

parameters.name: newTimeBasis
parameters.description: 'union' (default), 'intersection', 'commonrange', 'first', 'last', 'regular', or an explicit time vector.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Same fill, interpolation and aggregation methods as `retime`.

parameters.name: 'TimeStep'/'SampleRate'
parameters.description: Spacing when the basis is 'regular'.

tools.notes: The default 'union' basis with 'fillwithmissing' inserts NaN wherever a timetable has no sample, which is often what you want before interpolating. Variable names must be unique across the inputs.

tools.name: timerange
tools.description: Creates a time-range subscript object for selecting timetable rows whose row times fall within an interval. Use it inside timetable row subscripting to slice by time without constructing logical masks. Ranges can be specified by two endpoints or by a calendar unit such as a whole month.
tools.usage:
S = timerange(startTime, endTime)
S = timerange(startTime, endTime, intervalType)
S = timerange(t, unit)
TT(S, :)

parameters.name: startTime, endTime
parameters.description: Interval endpoints as datetime, duration or text.

parameters.name: intervalType
parameters.description: 'openright' (default), 'closed', 'open', 'openleft'.

parameters.name: unit
parameters.description: 'years', 'months', 'days', 'hours' and similar to select a whole calendar unit.

tools.notes: The default interval excludes the end point, so specify 'closed' when you want it included. `withtol` selects rows near given times within a tolerance, and `vartype` selects variables by class.

tools.name: categorical
tools.description: Creates a categorical array, which stores labelled discrete values efficiently and supports an optional meaningful ordering. Use it for grouping variables, factor levels and any repeated text labels, where it saves memory and enables comparison operators for ordinal data. Categories can be listed explicitly to fix their order and to catch unexpected values.
tools.usage:
B = categorical(A)
B = categorical(A, valueset)
B = categorical(A, valueset, catnames)
B = categorical(___, 'Ordinal', true)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Array of text, numbers or logicals to convert.

parameters.name: valueset
parameters.description: Values to map to categories, in the desired order.

parameters.name: catnames
parameters.description: Display names for each category.

parameters.name: 'Ordinal'
parameters.description: true to allow < and > comparisons between categories.

parameters.name: 'Protected'
parameters.description: true to prevent new categories being added by assignment.

tools.example:
g = categorical(["low";"high";"med";"low"], ["low","med","high"], 'Ordinal', true);
categories(g)
g > "low"
sort(g)
summary(g)
tools.notes: Values not present in the valueset become undefined (<undefined>) rather than raising an error, so check with `isundefined` after conversion. Ordinal categoricals support relational operators; non-ordinal ones support only equality.

tools.name: categories
tools.description: Returns the list of category names of a categorical array, in category order, as a cell array of character vectors. Use it to enumerate levels, to build legends and axis labels, and to verify that an import produced the expected set of labels. Unused categories are still listed.
tools.usage: C = categories(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Categorical array.

tools.notes: Categories persist even after all their members are removed, which keeps plots and summaries consistent; `removecats` drops unused ones. `renamecats`, `reordercats`, `addcats` and `mergecats` complete the category-management family.

tools.name: countcats
tools.description: Counts how many elements belong to each category of a categorical array, including categories with zero members. Use it for frequency tables, for checking class balance in labelled data, and for building bar charts of counts. The result is ordered by category order.
tools.usage:
B = countcats(A)
B = countcats(A, dim)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Categorical array.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which to count.

tools.example:
g = categorical(["a";"b";"a";"a";"c"]);
counts = countcats(g)
table(categories(g), num2cell(counts))
bar(categorical(categories(g)), counts)
tools.notes: Undefined elements are not counted in any category; count them separately with `sum(isundefined(g))`. `groupsummary` and `histogram` on categorical input give similar information with more formatting.

tools.name: reordercats
tools.description: Changes the order of the categories in a categorical array without changing which element belongs to which category. Use it to control the order of bars in a plot, the order of columns after `unstack`, and the meaning of comparisons in ordinal arrays. The new order must be a permutation of the existing categories.
tools.usage:
B = reordercats(A)
B = reordercats(A, newOrder)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Categorical array.

parameters.name: newOrder
parameters.description: Category names in the desired order.

tools.notes: Calling it with no order argument sorts categories alphabetically. Reordering is essential before plotting, because MATLAB draws categorical axes in category order, not in the order values first appear.

tools.name: discretize
tools.description: Assigns each data value to a bin defined by edges, a bin count, or a datetime unit, returning bin indices or a categorical array of bin names. Use it to convert continuous measurements into ordinal categories, to build lookup indices, and to prepare data for grouped analysis. Values outside the edges return NaN or undefined.
tools.usage:
Y = discretize(X, edges)
Y = discretize(X, N)
Y = discretize(X, dur)
[Y, E] = discretize(___)
C = discretize(___, 'categorical')
Y = discretize(___, values)

parameters.name: edges
parameters.description: Monotonically increasing bin edges; bins are left-closed except the last.

parameters.name: N
parameters.description: Number of uniform bins to create.

parameters.name: 'categorical'
parameters.description: Return a categorical array of bin names instead of indices.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Values to assign to each bin instead of an index.

parameters.name: 'IncludedEdge'
parameters.description: 'left' (default) or 'right'.

tools.example:
x = [1 5 9 12];
discretize(x, [0 5 10 15])
discretize(x, [0 5 10 15], 'categorical', {'low','mid','high'})
discretize(x, 2)
discretize(x, [0 5 10], [0 1])
tools.notes: Bins are half-open [a,b) except the last, which includes its right edge, matching `histcounts`. Values outside the outermost edges become NaN, which is easy to overlook.
